catalog_quote: ... grave, acute, or circumflex accent, seems to exist in two degrees: primary stress and secondary stress. The primary stress of a word is determined by the prosodic characteristics of the elements that make it up and, in particular, by the presence or absence of stressed suffixes. In fact, while prefixes are apparently all unstressed, suffixes can either be unstressed or bear the primary word stress. In words with one or more suffixes, primary stress can therefore fall on the root, as in atacá-ma-ra 'good (pl.)', or on its suffixal material, as in amukiri-méje 'I will play'. The placement of primary stress on the root cannot be predicted. Primary stress may fall on any one of its last three syllables, as the following verb roots indicate: kériri 'know', pedára 'be born', and penekà 'sit'.[n. 14] Probably due to the limitations of our material, no words minimally distinguished by primary word stress are attested. Secondary stress seems to be applied ... on at least one syllable to the left of the primary-stressed one (cf. akátuikè 'acknowledge'). ... when a stressed suffix is attached to a root ... the first accent would seem to reduce to secondary stress: híbitsche-rikíri [suffer-PAST1] 'he suffered' ...[n. 15] [Note 14] ... Most of the time, the stressed syllable in the root seems to be the penultimate. If two accented suffixes co-occur on a word, the main stress is likely to fall on the second of the two suffixes; compare tipe-dei-méje 'they will live forever'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Reconstructed from Baegert's (1772) inconsistent accent marks: primary stress is fixed by the morphemes present. Prefixes are never stressed; suffixes are lexically either stressed or unstressed. A word with a stressed suffix carries main stress on that suffix (the last one if two occur); otherwise main stress is on the root, usually on the root's penultimate syllable. Zamponi 2024 goes further: stress on roots cannot be predicted (kériri, pedára, penekà) and was probably phonemic.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Zamponi 2004 distinguishes primary and secondary stress ('seems to exist in two degrees'); fn. 15: in amukiri-méje 'I will play' the secondary stress on the root's penultimate syllable (cf. amukíri-re 'I play') is not even marked by Baegert.
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged throughout ('seems', 'most of the time', 'is likely'); Baegert's marking is 'not systematic' (2024); root stress not predictable per 2024 (kériri vs pedára vs penekà).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; inferred from a colonial catechism text (Lord's Prayer, Creed) and one verb paradigm, no audio or speaker data; Zamponi 2024 (De Gruyter chapter) is the newer statement and shifts toward lexical unpredictability of root stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Waikuri proper (Guaicurian, guai1237) as recorded by Baegert at Mission San Luis Gonzaga (1751-1768); Zamponi 2004 also draws minor data from Hostell and Ortega. Huchití/Uchití and Monqui are possibly related but distinct varieties (NOCODE); Pericú is unrelated. No dialect issue beyond this.

new_statements.quote: Given that the placement of stress (marked by Baegert, but not systematically, with a grave, acute, or circumflex accent) on roots cannot be predicted (kériri ‘know’, pedára ‘be born’, penekà ‘sit’), it is probable that stress was phonemically relevant in the language. [fn. 5:] As Shaul (2020: 42) notes, a nasal after a stressed vowel was probably longer than a nasal after an unstressed vowel; cf. apánne ‘great’, atacámmara ‘bad (pl.)’, and témme ‘while’ in the text of the Creed. [fn. 12, p. 110:] Both suffixes -ra and -me being unstressed, the primary-stressed syllable of the word can only be the first or the second syllable, not the final one.

new_statements.relation_note: Same author and same analysis as the existing Zamponi 2004 statement (root stress unpredictable, 'may fall on any one of its last three syllables', suffixes stressed or unstressed); the 2024 chapter is a condensed restatement using the same three examples and adds that stress was 'probably phonemically relevant'. Consistent with the catalog's classification lexical. Also gives a firm page (105) where the 2004 snippets had none.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress cannot be predicted on roots: Baegert's (unsystematic) accent marks place it on different syllables in different roots (kériri, pedára, penekà), so stress was probably phonemic (lexical). Some suffixes (-ra 'neg', -me 'fut1') are unstressed, so in a suffixed word primary stress stays on the root.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in this chapter (the 2004 article's secondary-stress remarks are not repeated here).
new_statements.exceptions: Baegert's accent marking is not systematic; fn. 12 treats the final grave in cuvu-me-rà as not indicating primary stress because -me and -ra are unstressed. Fn. 5: a nasal after a stressed vowel was probably longer (apánne, atacámmara, témme). Vowel length contrasts unrecoverable from Baegert's orthography.
new_statements.identity_note: Zamponi 2024 §5.1.3 concerns Waikuri proper as recorded by Baegert (1772; Lord's Prayer, Creed, verb paradigm from the Guaycura of the Magdalena plains / mission area), plus Dobrizhoffer's Per signum Crucis; the neighbouring Monqui (§5.1.1) and Pericú (§5.1.2) are treated as separate languages and say nothing about Waikuri stress. All stress statements are inferences from Baegert's German-based, unsystematic accent marks; no speaker data exist.

tone.quote: Stress does not define a phonological word. Instead, two stress patterns define a phrase or simple sentence (clause): weak-strong-(weak); strong-weak. Strong stress is marked (as Baegert did) with an acute accent. Secondary is marked (as Baegert did) with a grave accent. ... As may be seen, the Waikura stress patterning resembles a pitch-accent language like Japanese, Swedish, Salinan, or Keresan -- except that the prosodic unit is not a phonological word, but a phrase or clause.
tone.locator: pp. 32-33, Chapter 7, section 'Sound Pattern of Waikura'; cf. p. 31 'description of phrasal/clausal pitch accent intonation'
